text: Most people open Claude Code and use it like a chatbot. They ask a question, get an answer, and move on. That's the most common mistake we see. In the last topic, we called everything around the model the harness. Claude Code is that same loop, with a lot more software wrapped around it. And that software is the part you get to

shape. Here's a way to picture it. Say you can cook. So why not open a restaurant that serves a thousand people a day? Because you don't have the kitchen, the equipment or the staff to cook at that scale. The model is the cook. It's very good at one thing: writing the next piece of text. Everything around it is the kitchen.

That's the harness. And if all you need is one answer, you don't need a kitchen at all. You need one when the job takes steps, and actions, and a loop that keeps going until it's done. So let's walk into the kitchen, starting with the tools. The Parcelly agent you stepped through in the last topic had exactly one: lookup order. Claude Code comes with a whole

set. It can read files and write them, search through your project, run commands, and fetch a web page. And you can add more, through something called MCP, which we get to at the end of this module. The rule hasn't changed: the model asks for a tool, and the harness runs it. Next, the context.

In Claude Code, that's the system prompt, the chat so far, the files it has opened, and the result of every tool it ran. Plus a file called CLAUDE dot M D, which it loads at the start of every session. That's its memory of your project, and it's the next topic. Now, this context grows with every message, and you pay for all of it on every turn.

When it gets too full, the model starts to drift. It loses what you said at the start, and mixes old instructions into new work. So between tasks, type slash clear, and start fresh. Then there are permissions. The Parcelly agent trusted every tool call. Claude Code doesn't. Before it runs a command, deletes a file or

pushes to GitHub, it stops and asks you. So you get a moment to look before anything happens. Read what it's about to do, and say yes or no. If you can't tell what a command does, ask it. You can also set rules in advance: what it may always do, and what it must never do. So how do you actually work

with it? Mostly, you direct it, the way you'd direct a very fast engineer on your team. For anything bigger than a small change, start in plan mode. It writes a plan first. You read it, you push back, and only then do you let it build. Keep each request small:

one feature at a time. Read what it wrote, and ask it to walk you through a file until you could explain it to a client. And if it's trying the same fix over and over, stop it. Press escape, tell it what you noticed, and plan again. So here's the whole harness.

The model in the middle. Around it, the tools it can ask for, the context sent on every turn, the permissions that decide what it may do, and the memory that carries your project from one session to the next. And the loop running through all of it. When a session feels wrong, it's almost always one of those four.

Claude Code is one harness. Cursor, Cline, Codex and Lovable are others, around the same loop. In Module 3, you build one of your own. Now try it on something small. In your steps, switch Claude Code to plan mode and ask it to plan a one-page tip splitter. Read the plan, ask for one change,
and only then let it build. When it's done, ask it to walk you through what it wrote. Next: two ways to give this harness a memory of your project, CLAUDE dot M D and skills.
